A radar altimeter measures sea surface height by timing the round trip of a short microwave pulse between the spacecraft and the ocean. The instrument transmits at two frequencies so that the delay caused by free electrons in the ionosphere can be estimated and removed. The returned waveform is not a sharp spike; it is a smeared ramp whose shape depends on wave height, and a tracker fits a model to it to find the mean surface. Corrections are then applied for atmospheric water vapor, dry air pressure, tides, and the spacecraft's own orbital position, which is known to within a couple of centimeters using onboard GPS and laser tracking. After corrections, a single measurement has an uncertainty of a few centimeters, but averaging over many passes and regions reduces the error enough to detect changes of a few millimeters per year in global mean sea level.
